title: Afro-Descendants in the Independence
author: Felipe Ávila
content:
_This article by[Felipe
Ávila](https://www.jornada.com.mx/autores/Felipe%20%C3%81vila) originally
appeared in the [September 27, 2026 edition of La
Jornada](https://www.jornada.com.mx/noticia/2026/09/27/opinion/los-
afrodescendientes-en-la-independencia), Mexico's premier left wing daily
newspaper._

It has often been said that the War of Independence was a movement led by the
criollos, who culminated and capitalized on that process. It has been claimed
that the popular sectors were not clear about why they were fighting and only
followed their leaders, or chiefs, who came from the elites of New Spain.

However, it is necessary to stress that **the Independence of Mexico was a
great popular revolution** that was made possible by the participation of tens
of thousands of men and women from the poorest and most marginalized popular
sectors; who rose up in arms to fight not only for the Independence of Mexico,
but to build a more just and egalitarian society, putting an end to slavery,
to tribute and to the division into castes by social origin and skin color.
That is why they followed and fought alongside Hidalgo, Morelos, Guerrero and
many other insurgent leaders, because these leaders knew how to understand
their feelings and aspirations.

The poor people identified with them and formed a community that made possible
the triumph after 11 years of war that destroyed the foundations of the
colonial regime.

Those who swelled the insurgent ranks were above all **Indigenous people and
Afro-descendants, called negros or mulatos**. The massive participation of
entire peoples and communities was a cry of freedom and rebellion to put an
end to an oppressive social system that was imposed on them by force, that
destroyed a good part of their culture, that murdered many of their warriors
and priests, that raped their women, that prohibited their religious
practices, took away their lands and imposed on them a new political order, as
well as new laws, institutions, tributes, language and religion.

Those who suffered most from those abuses and humiliations were the Indigenous
and Afro-descendant communities, who managed to survive through constant
everyday resistance, many times hidden and other times open, with rebellions
that sought to improve their living conditions and defend their culture, their
traditions, their communal organization of labor, their traditional
authorities, their lands, forests and waters.

**The Independence of Mexico would not have been possible if the Indigenous
and Afro-descendant communities of the south of New Spain had not kept the
libertarian flame burning** after the execution of Morelos in December 1815.
In the most difficult years of the insurgent war, when its main leaders had
been killed, the resistance of the Indigenous people and Afro-descendants of
Tierra Caliente, of La Montaña and of the Costa Chica and Costa Grande of what
is today the state of Guerrero, as well as of the sierras of Puebla and
Oaxaca, kept up the struggle and could not be defeated by the royalist armies,
whose number reached 40,000 soldiers in those years.

In that southern region, the Indigenous and Afro-descendant communities had
supported Morelos in his military campaigns and had swelled the ranks of the
Galeana brothers and of Vicente Guerrero. They were communities and peoples
with a great identity and collective cohesion. The young men joined the
insurgent armies, while their fathers, mothers, grandparents, uncles and
siblings helped and committed themselves to the insurgent cause in different
ways.

The whole people was with them. That is why the royalist troops could not put
an end to that resistance. For that reason, they often burned villages,
executed their inhabitants en masse, imprisoned the women and deported the men
who were not in a condition to fight.

Vicente Guerrero was the most important insurgent leader of that period. He
had stood out for his bravery and military and organizational ability, and for
the backing he had from the Indigenous, Black and mulato communities of the
south of New Spain. **African blood ran through his veins.** He had made the
ideals of Hidalgo and Morelos his own.

He was a firm supporter of Independence, but also of establishing equality
among all, without distinction of ethnicity, wealth or skin color. The
abolition of slavery and of the division into castes, together with absolute
independence from Spain, were his main banners, and he had the unconditional
support of the Indigenous and Afro-descendant communities, who saw in him one
of their own.

Guerrero's army was made up mostly of Black and mulato men who made possible
the triumph of the insurgent cause. Among them was Juan del Carmen, a mulato
from Tlacoachistlahuaca, born in 1790, who joined Guerrero in 1811; he reached
the rank of colonel and took part in several of the main military operations
in La Montaña and the Costa Chica between 1812 and 1817. Guerrero held him in
esteem and made him his lieutenant.

The troops of Guerrero and Juan del Carmen had a broad knowledge of the
terrain: rugged sierras, deep ravines and the bravery of the guerrillas made
them unbeatable. One tactic that worked for them was to establish
fortifications in towns or villages high in the sierra. Mothers, wives,
children and relatives of the combatants took refuge there. They set up small
factories for munitions and cannons; they had blacksmith shops, carpentry
shops; the civilian population helped with different tasks.

The royalist armies, which outnumbered them in soldiers and weaponry, could
not defeat them. Thus the resistance was sustained between 1815 and 1821. One
of the main forts was on the hill of Xonacatlán, where Juan del Carmen had 300
combatants. In March 1817, the viceroy sent a strong military contingent
against that small fort. It took them a month to defeat the rebels. Juan del
Carmen died on March 3.

It was a great loss for the insurgent cause. Guerrero stated that it was not
for lack of courage, but for lack of food and water, that they had been
defeated, and he erected a memorial in the church of San Pedro in Xonacatlán,
in honor of Juan del Carmen, where he is still remembered today.
